passage: It's been a month since Salma and I sat down with our manager and wrote out the agreement, and I, Kiran, didn't expect it to hold. Three lines on one page: Salma owns client calls, I own the analysis; both names go on every deck, in alphabetical order; if something bothers either of us, we say it within two days, privately. Honestly, the third line was the hardest. Two weeks in, Salma moved a deadline without telling me, and the old me would have stewed for a month. Instead I messaged: 'Can we talk about Thursday?' It took ten minutes. Yesterday we had our one-month check-in over chai. We both laughed at how much energy we'd wasted being silently angry. Next time I'll speak up in week one, not month three.

qa.q: Whose names go on every deck, and in what order?
qa.a: Both names go on every deck, in alphabetical order.

qa.q: Why was the third line of the agreement the hardest for Kiran?
qa.a: Speaking up within two days went against Kiran's old habit of stewing silently, so it felt uncomfortable and risky.

qa.q: What made this agreement actually work?
qa.a: It was short and specific about ownership, credit and raising concerns, and it was tested early with a ten-minute talk and a one-month check-in.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt receiving 'Can we talk about Thursday?'
qa.a: Salma may have felt a moment of worry but also relief that the issue came directly and quickly, rather than turning into weeks of coldness.

grounding: Two colleagues agree on ownership, shared credit and raising concerns early, check in after a month, and see the conflict as a lesson in speaking sooner.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Raghav, one month after the Hemant and Nisha agreement.
What they agreed in March: Hemant owns vendor contracts, Nisha owns the budget sheet; credit on reports names both, with each person's part listed; any concern gets raised within the week, first with each other, then with me if needed.
What I saw: two emails this month opened with 'Flagging early...' One from Nisha about a late invoice, one from Hemant about a formula. Both were sorted the same day. The team report went out with a short line under each section: who did what.
At today's check-in, Hemant said, 'If we'd done this in January, we'd have saved ourselves the shouting.' Nisha nodded.
Next: suggest the whole team uses the same ownership sheet.

qa.q: What did Nisha's early email flag?
What does Hemant's comment about January suggest about Hemant's thinking now?
qa.a: Hemant seems to regret not speaking up sooner and sees the conflict as a lesson in raising concerns early.

qa.q: Why is Raghav's next step, sharing the ownership sheet, a good idea?
qa.a: It spreads what worked, clear ownership and early flagging, so the rest of the team can prevent similar conflicts.

qa.q: How might Nisha experience a report that lists who did what?
qa.a: Nisha likely feels the work is visible and fairly credited, which builds trust instead of resentment.

grounding: A supervisor records how clear ownership, shared credit and early flagging held up at a one-month check-in, turning a past clash into a lesson.
